newsitem.title: CHINA: China stocks plunge on quota, but rebound seen.
newsitem.headline: China stocks plunge on quota, but rebound seen.

text.p: China's stock prices plunged in early trade on Friday after Beijing announced a huge quota for stock issues in 1997, but later recovered some ground on good market fundamentals, brokers said.
A few minutes after the opening, Shanghai's A share index had slumped 51.157 points or 3.45 percent to 1,432.086 points and the B share index had shed 2.199 points or 2.48 percent to 86.571 points.
In Shenzhen, the A index initially lost 17.73 points or 3.44 percent to 497.74 points and the B index shed 3.79 points or 2.20 percent to 168.73 points.
But the indices trimmed losses at mid-morning as investors recovered from the shock of the sudden announcement of the market expansion plan, brokers said.

By 0330 GMT, Shanghai's A share index was down 32.936 points or 2.22 percent to 1450.307 points after plunging 7.82 percent at the opening. The city's B share index was off 1.64 percent to 87.314 points.
By late morning the Shenzhen A index was down 3.55 percent to 497.19 points after opening down 8.51 percent. The B index was off 2.40 percent to 168.38.

A shares are reserved for mainland Chinese investors. B shares are theoretically restricted to foreigners, although Chinese nationals have found ways around the rules and account for more than half of the B share market's daily turnover.

The Securities Commission under the State Council (cabinet) and the State Planning Commission on Thursday announced a quota for new stock issues in 1997 of 30 billion yuan, double the 1996 quota of 15 billion.

Brokers said the market had been unprepared for such a huge quota and had not expected Beijing to announce this year's quota so soon. China usually announces each year's share listing quota at the end of the year.
"Investors were caught completely unprepared for such an announcement," said one trader. "Panic selling emerged in the first few minutes of trading."
But brokers said market fundamentals were still good as China's economy was improving and listed firms were expected to post better results for the year.
Brokers said the indices were likely to claw back more ground later in the day.

"The indices will recover to some extent for the rest of the session today with good market fundamentals changing little," said a broker. "The indices are likely to move in negative territory for the day but the loss margin might be trimmed to around two percent."
China's decision to double the new stock issue quota in 1997 from 1996 aims to increase the supply of stocks and curb overheating on the stock markets, the China Securities News said on Friday.
The move is also aimed at bolstering major state-run firms, which will be given priority for share listings, the newspaper said in a commentary.
"The unprecedented large-scale quota indicates the authorities intend to curb the over-heated stock markets by effectively increasing stock supply," the commentary said.

The newspaper said there had been an acute shortage of shares on China's stock markets in the past year with more and more investors wanting to invest due to the healthy development of the nation's economy.
This had resulted in sharp rises in stock prices and some excessive speculation, the newspaper said.
